newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - South African growth, rand descent to slow - poll.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - South African growth, rand descent to slow - poll.

text.p: South African economic growth will slow to just 2.2 percent in 1997 from 3.0 in 1996 but the balance of payments is set to improve and the rand's descent will slow, according to a survey published on Thursday.
The poll of 28 economists by Reuters, conducted after last week's one-point rise in the central bank's key Bank Rate to 17 percent, found an already weak economy set to slow further.
"Domestic demand is already slowing but a particular slowdown in private consumption expenditure will be magnified by the rate hike," said Julia Roy, Treasury economist at Rand Merchant Bank.
Figures released on Thursday showed the South African economy grew by an annualised 3.2 percent in the third quarter, down from 3.7 percent in the second quarter.
Excluding agriculture, which was boosted by a bumper maize crop, the core economy grew just 0.5 percent quarter on quarter.
For 1998, economists expect some improvement, as the business cycle turns, but the consensus growth forecast of 3.15 percent remains well below the level hoped for by government.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's macro-economic strategy, unveiled in June, had projected growth of 2.9 percent in 1997 and 3.8 percent in 1998, en route to 6.1 percent in 2000.

The growth slowdown should allow a reversal of the November 21 rate rise in the first half of next year and over the next two years interest rates could be cut by up to five percentage points, economists said.
The yawning deficit on the current account of the balance of payments should narrow sharply as weak domestic demand limits imports and the fall in the rand gives exports a fillip.
The consensus forecast for the current account gap in 1997 was 4.63 billion rand, less than half the expected 10.13 billion deficit this year and against a 12.7 billion deficit in 1995.
That, in turn, should help stabilise the rand after its 30 percent plunge against the U.S. dollar this year.
The consensus forecast was for an exchange rate for the rand of 4.92 against the dollar by the end of 1997, and 5.17 by the end of the following year.

Some analysts even expected the currency to appreciate in 1997 -- despite South Africa's higher inflation rate compared to its major trading partners -- with the most bullish forecast being a rate of 4.42 by end-1997.
The rand was last trading at around 4.55/4.56 against the dollar.

"I think the fact that we are seeing the rand stabilising for longer periods at certain levels indicates that maybe the downward pressure has run out of steam," said Johan Rossouw, economist at stockbroker Huysamer Stals.
"On a fundamental basis it is clearly undervalued. The question is just when will it start making headway again and to what extent."
The survey forecast consumer price inflation would remain under control in 1997, despite the fall in the rand, averaging 8.94 percent following an average of 7.48 percent in 1996.
That should help underpin government bond prices, although economists did not forecast any major downward move in yields.

The results of the survey showed the yield on the benchmark R150 long bond was expected to reach 15.44 percent in the first quarter of 1997 and shed a further 90 basis points by the end of next year. The R150 was last yielding 15.75 percent.
